content: The study was conducted during the 1997-1998 influenza season, a period when the vaccine and circulating A (H3N2) strains were not well-matched. During peak outbreak periods, no significant difference in febrile illnesses was observed between recipients of the live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) and those who received a placebo. However, vaccination was associated with a 19% reduction in severe febrile illnesses and a 24% reduction in febrile upper respiratory tract illnesses. Vaccination also resulted in fewer days of illness, fewer days of work lost, fewer healthcare provider visits, and reduced use of both prescription antibiotics and over-the-counter medications. Among a subset of 3,637 healthy adults aged 18-49 years, those who received LAIV (n = 2,411) experienced 26% fewer episodes of febrile upper respiratory tract illness, 27% fewer workdays lost due to febrile upper respiratory tract illness, and 18%-37% fewer days of healthcare provider visits for febrile illnesses compared to placebo recipients (n = 1,226). Additionally, days of antibiotic use were reduced by 41%-45% in this age group. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled challenge study involving 92 healthy adults aged 18-41 years (LAIV, n = 29; placebo, n = 31; inactivated influenza vaccine, n = 32) evaluated the efficacy of both LAIV and the inactivated vaccine. The overall efficacy of LAIV and the inactivated influenza vaccine in preventing laboratory-confirmed influenza from all three strains combined was 85% and 71%, respectively, based on experimental challenge with viruses to which participants were susceptible prior to vaccination. The difference in efficacy between the two vaccines was not statistically significant. Influenza vaccination has been shown to reduce both healthcare costs and productivity losses associated with influenza illness. Studies conducted in the United States among individuals aged >65 years have reported significant reductions in hospitalizations, deaths, and overall societal cost savings. Among adults aged <65 years, vaccination has been shown to reduce direct medical costs and indirect costs from work absenteeism. Reported reductions include 13%-44% in healthcare provider visits, 18%-45% in lost workdays, 18%-28% in days working with reduced effectiveness, and 25% in antibiotic use for influenza-associated illnesses. One cost-effectiveness analysis estimated the cost of preventing an influenza illness among healthy individuals aged 18-64 years to range from $60 to $4,000, depending on the cost of vaccination, the influenza attack rate, and vaccine effectiveness against influenza-like illness (ILI). Another study estimated a cost of $66 per person vaccinated. In one analysis, 78% of all costs prevented were attributed to reduced productivity losses from work, whereas another study did not include productivity losses in its calculations. Economic studies specifically evaluating the cost-effectiveness of vaccinating individuals aged 50-64 years are not available, and there are limited studies examining the economics of routinely vaccinating children with trivalent inactivated vaccine (TIV) or LAIV. Cost per year of healthy life gained improved with increasing age and among those with chronic medical conditions. Among individuals aged >65 years, vaccination resulted in net savings per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained, whereas among younger age groups, vaccination resulted in costs of $23-$256 per QALY. In addition to estimating the economic costs associated with influenza disease, studies have assessed public perceptions of preventing influenza morbidity. Less than half of respondents in a survey on public perception of the value of preventing influenza morbidity indicated they would trade any time from their own life to prevent a case of uncomplicated influenza in a hypothetical child. When asked about their willingness to pay to prevent a hypothetical child from having an uncomplicated case of influenza, the median willingness-to-pay amount was $100 for a 14-year-old child and $175 for a 1-year-old child. One of the national health objectives for 2010 was to achieve an influenza vaccination coverage level of 90% for individuals aged >65 years. Among this age group, influenza vaccination levels increased from 33% in 1989 to 66% in 1999, surpassing the Healthy People 2000 objective of 60%. Vaccination coverage in this group reached its highest recorded level (68%) during the 1999-2000 influenza season. This estimate was based on the percentage of adults reporting influenza vaccination during the previous 12 months in the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). The NHIS, administered during the first and second quarters of each calendar year, was used as a proxy measure of influenza vaccination coverage for the previous influenza season.
